# Matthieu Duchatellier

Source: https://matthieu.pm

# Matthieu Duchatellier

Product Manager · Design Engineer

I love building AI products. Making my own, like Forge and Carbon, has taught me a lot about engineering, and it’s changed how I approach product and design. Currently, I'm pursuing a Product Management & UX Design MSc at SKEMA & POLIMI.

Previously, I worked on growth and product design at [**Avico**](<https://www.avico.com/en/>), an air charter broker, and [**Xllence**](<https://www.xllence.fr/fr/>), a B2B sales agency. I’m open to a Product Manager or Design Engineer role starting June 2027.

You can reach me at [**@matthieu\_pm**](<https://x.com/matthieu_pm>) or via ** email  mattduchatellier@gmail.com ** and explore my code on [**GitLab**](<https://gitlab.com/wondertale-dev>).

## Tools and apps I built

-   [**My collection** ~ Curated lists of tools and inspiring designs](<https://matthieu.pm/inspirations>)
-   [**Atlas** ~ Prepare your exams with AI-powered MCQs](<https://atlasapp.fr/>)
-   [**Atrium** ~ Revenue teams meet agentic CRM workflows](<https://atriumcrm.com/>)
-   [**Carbon** ~ A desktop home for your coding agents](<https://carbonhq.sh/>)

# HomeView — a home display concept

Source: https://matthieu.pm/archive/homeview

Archive · Design study

# HomeView

A small display. A little more life at home.

An Apple-inspired home display with a square screen, an aluminum enclosure, and a domed speaker base. A study in making a physical object feel tangible and usable in the browser.

## Explore the concept

 My Home ◔

Living room

 21°

 Feels just right

−+

 **Lights** 3 lights on  ♫**Music** A moment of calm

Choose a finish below the device. Swipe its screen, or focus the display and use the arrow keys, to explore Home, Music, and Clock. Try the lights, temperature controls, and music animation.

## Start with the object

The concept brings a few everyday actions into one quiet object: adjust the room temperature, switch the lights, or glance at the time. The music screen adds an animated player. These controls simulate the experience locally; they don’t connect to home devices or play audio.

The hardware takes cues from Apple’s materials and proportions. This is an independent design study, unaffiliated with Apple, with model units rather than manufactured dimensions.

## Build the form in code

The device is drawn with SVG. A build script uses the Anatomy geometry kit to project 47 solids into a shared view: the rubber foot, speaker body, 36 curved grille segments, dome, hinge, and layered display. The speaker apertures follow the curved surface, while the bezel and glass share the display’s rounded outline.

The script orders and audits the geometry, then saves the paths in a generated file. Next.js renders those paths on the server. The browser receives the finished shapes, so it doesn’t need to rebuild the hardware during an animation.

SVG

The enclosure, speaker, shadows, and material detail.

HTML + CSS

A live screen aligned to the same projected plane.

React

Screen navigation, finishes, and local control states.

## Put a real interface on the screen

The screen is HTML positioned over the SVG device with a shared transformation matrix. That keeps text and buttons interactive while matching the angle of the glass. It also avoids a WebKit rendering issue with layered HTML inside an SVG foreignObject.

Swipes are translated from the pointer’s position into the screen’s own coordinates. The interface follows the drag, then settles onto a screen using distance and flick velocity. A little resistance at either end makes the boundary feel physical. Keyboard navigation offers the same three screens, and inactive screens are removed from the focus order.

## Finish with the small details

Four finishes change the material colors through CSS variables. The swatches sit outside the card so the object stays the focus. Moving the pointer shifts a soft reflection across the glass, the lights update their readout, and the clock uses the visitor’s local time.

The device and screen scale together as the card gets smaller. Motion respects reduced-motion preferences, and the clock updates only while the concept is in view. The result pairs a fixed, detailed illustration with a small layer of live behavior.

[Back to Archive](<https://matthieu.pm/#archive-title>) Matthieu Duchatellier

# My collection

A collection of inspiring interfaces, component libraries, AI tools, and resources for bringing ideas to life.

## My stack

- [Figma](<https://figma.com/>): Collaborative interface design and prototyping platform.
- [tldraw](<https://tldraw.com/>): Infinite whiteboard and canvas SDK.
- [Aside browser](<https://aside.com/>): A browser with an AI assistant for working across websites.
- [Maze](<https://maze.co/>): User research and usability testing platform.
- [PostHog](<https://posthog.com/>): Product analytics, session replay, and experimentation tools.
- [Linear](<https://linear.app/>): Project management software setting speed standards.
- [Codex](<https://openai.com/codex/>): OpenAI coding agent for building, debugging, and reviewing code.
- [Ghostty](<https://ghostty.org/>): Fast GPU-accelerated terminal emulator for developers.
- [GitLab](<https://about.gitlab.com/>): Git repositories, code review, and continuous integration.
- [Bun](<https://bun.com/>): JavaScript runtime, package manager, bundler, and test runner.
- [TypeScript](<https://www.typescriptlang.org/>): JavaScript with syntax for types.
- [Rust](<https://rust-lang.org/>): A programming language for reliable and efficient software.
- [Tauri](<https://tauri.app/>): Build cross-platform apps with Rust and web technologies.
- [React](<https://react.dev/>): A library for building web and native user interfaces.
- [Next.js](<https://nextjs.org/>): A React framework for building web applications.
- [TanStack](<https://tanstack.com/>): Open-source libraries for building web applications.
- [shadcn/ui](<https://ui.shadcn.com/>): Components you copy directly into codebases.
- [NeonDB](<https://neon.com/>): Serverless Postgres with database branching and autoscaling.
- [Convex](<https://www.convex.dev/>): Reactive backend with a database, TypeScript functions, and realtime sync.
- [Vercel](<https://vercel.com/>): Cloud platform for deploying Next.js applications.
- [Notion](<https://www.notion.com/>): A workspace for notes, documents, and projects.

Color palette generators, contrast checkers, and color math.

- [Orbkit](<https://orbkit.zzzzshawn.cloud/>): WebGL shader renderer for orb animations.

## Icons

# Great UI

Source: https://matthieu.pm/skills/great-ui

# /great-ui

Make every interface detail feel right.

A faithful merge of [Better UI](<https://github.com/jakubkrehel/skills/tree/main/skills/better-ui>) and [Emil Design Engineering](<https://github.com/emilkowalski/skills/tree/main/skills/emil-design-eng>). It brings together surfaces, icons, and motion that feel right.

`npx skills add matthieu-pm/great-ui`

## Correct is the start. Crafted is the goal.

Refine the details that make an interface feel intentional. Improve geometry, optical balance, and surface depth. Add contextual icons, generous hit areas, and subtle motion.

 Message

 Day  Week  Month

 1,201

 Follow

 Message

 Day  Week  Month

 1,201

## Make the geometry feel inevitable.

Nested surfaces feel related when their radii share the same center. Adjust each value to see the geometry respond in real time.

 Outer radius

20px 20

 Inner radius

12px 12

 Padding

8px 8

Change the values to see how the border radius adapts.

## Polish is a system, not a flourish.

Great UI combines both source skills rather than selecting a few memorable tricks.

### Surfaces

The same reading card, with geometry and depth that feel related.

Without skill

#### Words that work.

Small details. Clearer interfaces.

With skill

#### Words that work.

Small details. Clearer interfaces.

Concentric corners, balanced spacing, and layered shadows replace mismatched radii and hard outlines.

### Interaction

Not saved yet

With skill

Not saved yet

Press feedback, smooth icon changes, and a picker anchored to its button make each action feel connected.

### Restraint

The same filter, with the unnecessary motion taken away.

Without skill

-    **Words that work** — Writing
-    **A little less motion** — Interaction
-    **Details add up** — Craft

 3 notes

-    **A little less motion** — Interaction
-    **Details add up** — Craft

 3 notes

Removing the repeated entrance animation makes filtering immediate and keeps attention on the content.

## Two perspectives. One working method.

Better UI supplies exact recipes. Emil Design Engineering supplies the judgment for when and why to use them.

01 **better-ui** — Exact values for surfaces, icons, and motion.

02 **emil-design-eng** — Craft judgment, interaction purpose, and restraint.

https://github.com/emilkowalski/skills/tree/main/skills/emil-design-eng

# Write the interface

Source: https://matthieu.pm/writing/ux-writing

# Write the interface

Learn to write labels, buttons, and messages that help people use your product. Practice with ten short exercises.

 By Matthieu Duchatellier

## Help people take the next step

UX writing helps people understand what a product does and how to use it. A button names an action. A field label explains what to enter. An error message helps someone recover when a task fails.

Compare “Submit” with “Save changes.” The second label tells you what will happen. That is the job of interface copy: give people enough information to act with confidence.

Use this guide to choose clearer labels, write helpful messages, and review a product flow. Try the exercises as you go, or read through first. All examples are for practice.

 Try it · Profile settings

 Display name

This is how your name appears on your profile.

Alex Morgan

 Save changes

UX writing names the action: “Save changes.” Content design decides which fields belong together and where the confirmation appears.

## Recognize microcopy

**Microcopy** is the short text that guides an interaction. Its purpose matters more than its length: a slogan attracts attention, while a password hint helps someone finish a task.

 Onboarding  Empty state  Notification  Tooltip  Success message  Title  Button label  Confirmation  Label  Progress update  Alert  Transactional email

These words appear in apps, websites, kiosks, and voice assistants. At each step, ask: what does the person need to know now, and what can they do next?

## Find the microcopy

Choose the examples that help someone use a product. You can select more than one.

Which examples guide a product interaction? Select all that apply.

 Error message  Tooltip  Onboarding step  Call to action  Blog post  Advertising slogan

 0 selected  Check answer

## Write while you design

UX writers work closely with designers, product managers, researchers, developers, support, and marketing. Start with the user’s goal and write the copy while the flow is still taking shape.

 Discover

Listen to users. Collect their words and questions.

 Build

Write in the prototype. Check each action and state.

 Deliver

Test understanding. Improve and document the copy.

Review the flow together. Can someone skip this step? What happens if saving fails? Does “Delete” mean permanent deletion? Agree on the behavior before writing a promise the product cannot keep.

## Give every word a job

Review your draft in four passes. Start with what the person needs, then make the wording shorter, more natural, and easier to understand.

**Purposeful** — Does it help someone decide, act, or recover?

**Concise** — Can you cut words without losing needed context?

**Conversational** — Would you say this to someone asking for help?

**Clear** — Will people understand what happens next?

Shorter is not always clearer. “File too large” names the problem. “Choose a file under 10 MB” also explains how to fix it. Keep the details someone needs to finish the task.

## Choose a helpful error message

Compare the messages. Which one explains what to do next?

An upload paused when the internet connection dropped. The product can resume it. Which message helps someone continue?

 Option A **Something went wrong.** — Please try again later.  Option B **Upload paused** — Your connection dropped. Reconnect, then resume the upload.

## Replace the jargon

Rewrite this sign-in error in everyday language. Explain the problem and give a next step.

 Replace this

Authentication was unsuccessful due to invalid credentials.

 Your sign-in message

The email and password don’t match. Help someone check their details and try again. Limit: 180 characters.

 180 characters left  Compare with an example

## Put the important words first

Put the most important information first. Use short sentences, active voice, and familiar words. If a technical term is essential, explain it where it appears. If it is not essential, replace it.

 Lead with the action  Use active voice  Use everyday words  Write for translation

 Example · Email and account messages

 Before

To continue, you will need to verify your email.

 After

### Verify your email to continue

Open the verification link we sent to alex@example.com.

The heading puts the next action first. The supporting line explains how to complete it.

## Keep one name

A workspace, project, and space may sound like different things. Keep one name for the same concept.

 Navigation **Workspace**

 Page title **Your project**

 Confirmation **Space created**

All three labels describe the same thing. What should the team do?

 Choose one term  Keep the variety  Add tooltips

## Match the words to the component

Start with the question someone has at that moment. What will this button do? Why is this list empty? Did my changes save? Use the component to answer it.

**Button**

Name the action and object: “Save changes” or “Download invoice.”

**Loading**

Describe the current task: “Uploading your file…” Only show progress you can measure.

**Onboarding**

Explain one useful step: “Choose a language to find lessons.”

**Empty state**

Explain what belongs here: “No saved places yet. Save a place to find it here later.”

**Success**

Confirm the result: “Changes saved.” Add a next step only if one is needed.

**Error**

Name the problem and a way forward: “Upload failed. Choose a file under 10 MB.”

Put essential instructions beside the action. Give form fields visible labels, and keep requirements outside placeholders that disappear during typing. Offer extra detail when it is useful.

For errors, explain the cause only when you know it. Say what was saved or charged only when the product can confirm it. Before a permanent action, state the consequence and name both choices: “Delete draft” and “Keep draft.”

## Name the button’s action

Choose a label that matches what the button actually does.

 Hotel search

The button only checks whether rooms are available. It does not make a booking.

What should the button say?

 Book a room  Check availability  Continue

## Build an error message

Choose the details someone needs after a failed payment. Then review an example message.

 Card payment failed

The order is still in the basket and nothing has been charged. The person can try another payment method. The cause is unknown.

Which details belong in the error message? Select all that apply.

 What happened  How to recover  What was saved  The internal error code  Who caused the problem

 0 selected  Check answer

## Test the words in the flow

A UX writing audit reviews a complete journey, not isolated sentences. Capture the screen, component, current copy, user goal, issue, proposed change, and evidence. Fix the problems that prevent someone from finishing before polishing less important wording.

Test important language in a prototype with the people who will use it. Watch whether they understand the state, predict the action, and recover from problems. For high-volume decisions, compare variants with an A/B test. For example, test whether a clearer booking label helps people find a room. Check completed bookings and accidental actions as well as clicks.

 Try it · File upload

### Your file is too large

trip-notes.pdf is 12 MB. Choose a file under 10 MB.

 Use a smaller example file

Can you explain why the upload failed, predict the next action, and finish without help? The file name stays consistent throughout.

## Find the copy problems

Review this error screen. Select every issue that makes it harder to understand or recover.

 Profile transfer **Migration unsuccessful**

A synchronization exception occurred.

 Continue

Which problems affect this screen? Select all that apply.

 Vague button label  Internal jargon  No next step  Long page title

 0 selected  Check audit

## Use words your readers recognize

Good interface language begins with evidence: interviews, support conversations, search queries, reviews, usability sessions, and the words people already use. Collect repeated phrases and the context in which they appear. Use them to propose labels, then test whether other people understand those labels in the product.

A useful persona is not a fictional biography. It captures the user’s goal, situation, knowledge, anxieties, and vocabulary. Write for the decisions that person needs to make in the product.

## Find the user’s language

Read the fictional research excerpts. Choose a label that reflects the words these people use.

“I want to find the places I saved for later.”

“Where did my saved places go?”

“I save restaurants before a trip.”

What should the navigation label say?

 Repository  Saved places  My collection

## Adjust the tone to the situation

Voice is the product’s consistent personality. Tone adapts that voice to the situation. A celebration can be energetic; a payment problem should be calm and specific. Consider the person’s goal, likely concerns, and the consequences of the action.

 Routine confirmation

 Changes saved

Confirm the result. Keep it brief.

 First use

### No saved places yet

Save a place to find it before your next trip.

Explain what belongs here and how to start.

 Something failed

### We couldn’t load your places

Check your connection, then try again.

Name the problem and give a recovery step.

 Permanent action

### Delete “Weekend in Paris”?

This deletes the list and its saved places. You can’t undo this.

State exactly what will be lost.

Document your voice with examples. If it is clear, warm, and direct, show how those qualities work in a welcome, an error, and a confirmation. Keep humor out of moments when someone may lose work or money.

## Choose a tone that fits

Try both situations. Choose a message that respects how the person may be feeling.

 Payment delayed  Goal reached

A bank transfer is taking longer than expected. The product will notify the sender when it completes.

 A Woohoo! Your payment is taking a little adventure.  B Your transfer is still processing. We’ll let you know when it’s complete.  C Transfer pending. Wait.

## Document the decisions you repeat

A content design system is the shared source of truth for interface language. Start with the decisions your team keeps making: which terms to use, how to explain errors, and what each button should say.

 Example · A reusable content pattern

### When someone saves a place

Use a short confirmation. Keep the feature name “Saved places” in navigation and help text.

 Added to your saved places

Use after saving succeeds. If saving fails, explain the problem and offer a retry. Avoid “Repository” and “Collection” for this feature.

Owner: the team responsible for saved places.

Store the wording, its intended use, and its owner together. Review the pattern when the product behavior changes.

A glossary entry can be simple: “Saved places” means places someone has bookmarked. Use it in navigation and headings; avoid “Repository” for the same feature. Include the reason, an owner, and a review date.

## Remove barriers to understanding

Accessible UX writing uses plain language, descriptive labels, short sentences, and context that does not depend on vision, color, or prior knowledge. Check whether someone can understand the task while using a screen reader, reading in a second language, or working in a hurry.

Do not communicate meaning through color, position, sound, or imagery alone. Write links and buttons that make sense out of context. Name the field with a visible label. Explain errors next to the affected input.

 Try it · Delivery details

### Choose your delivery date

1.  Enter an email address for delivery updates.
2.  Choose a future delivery date.

 Email address  (Required) name@example.com

Use a made-up address to try this example.

 Delivery date  (Required)

Try a past date to see the error message.

Read the delivery policy

For this example, any future date is available. In a real checkout, explain available days and delivery costs here.

 Save delivery details

The labels stay visible while you type. Required fields use text, the date error explains the fix, and the policy link names its destination. Nothing is sent or booked.

Inclusion goes further than technical access. Avoid assumptions about gender, relationships, ability, culture, or available resources. Ask only for information the task truly needs, and do not encode a presumed user into labels or defaults. “Emergency contact” leaves room for more relationships than “Husband or wife.”

In a voice or conversational interface, language becomes the interface. Explain what it understood, confirm consequential actions, and let people correct mistakes.

## Remove the barrier

Compare two form instructions. Choose the one people can understand without seeing color.

A form has three required fields. Which instruction removes the most barriers?

 Option A **Complete the fields in red.** — Required information is communicated through color.  Option B **Complete all fields marked “Required”.** — Each field also includes a visible text label.

## Use AI to draft alternatives

AI can generate alternatives, challenge a tone, simplify complex text, group feedback, or help review a flow. Give it the user’s goal, the product’s actual behavior, the component, and any constraints. Include examples of your voice and preferred terms.

Treat every output as a draft. Verify the product behavior, source claims, accessibility, terminology, tone, and privacy before anything ships. A strong workflow asks for several options, compares them against explicit criteria, and improves the brief from the failures.

## Try it on one screen

Choose a screen in your product. Write down what someone needs to do, revise the words that might slow them down, and ask another person what they expect to happen next.

[Matthieu Duchatellier](<https://matthieu.pm/>) Writing about product, design, and AI.

# From Prompt to Product

Source: https://matthieu.pm/writing/ai-design-engineer

# From Prompt to Product

A hands-on introduction to prompting, building, and refining interfaces with AI.

 By Matthieu Duchatellier

## AI is a fast collaborator, not an art director.

Use it to create options, translate intent into code, and inspect the result. Keep the taste, constraints, and final judgment with you.

## Start with a visual brief

Name the user, the job, the mood, the hierarchy, and the constraints. A precise brief beats a long prompt.

## Ask for different directions

Generate three meaningfully different approaches before polishing one. Compare structure, not decoration.

## Build in small slices

Move from layout to components to states. Review each slice in the browser before adding more.

## Critique with evidence

Check screenshots at real breakpoints. Ask what is unclear, inconsistent, inaccessible, or visually weak.

## Polish by hand

Fix spacing, type, motion, focus states, and edge cases. AI gets you to a draft; craft gets you to done.

[Matthieu Duchatellier](<https://matthieu.pm/>) Writing about product, design, and AI.

---

# The AI-Augmented Product Manager

Source: https://matthieu.pm/writing/ai-product-manager

# The AI-Augmented Product Manager

A practical guide for PMs using AI to sharpen discovery, decisions, and delivery.

 By Matthieu Duchatellier

## Use AI to widen the work, not outsource the decision.

AI can compress research, challenge assumptions, and sharpen product artifacts. Your job is still to supply context and own the tradeoffs.

## Give it the real context

Share the goal, user, constraints, evidence, and open questions. Generic context creates generic advice.

## Synthesize, then verify

Use AI to cluster interviews or feedback, but trace every important claim back to the source.

## Generate counterarguments

Ask what would make the idea fail, which assumption is weakest, and what cheaper test could prove it.

## Draft sharper artifacts

Turn decisions into briefs, specs, test plans, and release notes. Edit for product truth and team clarity.

## Keep a decision log

Record the evidence, tradeoff, owner, and revisit date. AI is most useful when the reasoning stays visible.

[Matthieu Duchatellier](<https://matthieu.pm/>) Writing about product, design, and AI.

# Connect your assistant

Source: https://matthieu.pm/mcp

# Good references.
One connection.

Bring my design collection, skills, and writing into the conversation you’re already having with your AI assistant.

## Connect with MCP

MCP lets compatible AI assistants use resources from other apps and websites. Add this site as a remote MCP server in your assistant’s connection settings.

1.  Choose the option to add a remote or custom MCP server.
2.  Name it **Matthieu’s resources** and paste this server URL.
3.  If asked, choose **Streamable HTTP** and no authentication.

`https://matthieu.pm/mcp` Copy

Your assistant needs to support remote MCP servers without authentication. The option and its name depend on the app you use.

Using Codex from the terminal?

Run this command to add the connection:

`codex mcp add matthieu --url https://matthieu.pm/mcp` Copy

## Start with a question

Once connected, try asking your assistant:

-   “Find typography resources in Matthieu’s design collection.”
-   “Read Matthieu’s Great UI guide and suggest improvements to this interface.”
-   “Find Matthieu’s writing on UX copy and help me improve these error messages.”

## What you can use

[The design collection ↗](<https://matthieu.pm/inspirations>)

Search curated tools, interface inspiration, components, visuals, utilities, and design engineers.

[Skills ↗](<https://matthieu.pm/skills/great-ui>)

Read the published Great UI guide, its examples, and installation instructions.

[Writing ↗](<https://matthieu.pm/writing/ux-writing>)

Search and read articles on UX writing, building interfaces with AI, and AI for product managers.

Available tools and resources

`search_collection`

Find resources by keyword or category.

`search_content`

Search the full text of published skills and articles. An empty query lists the pages.

`get_content`

Read a page as Markdown using its ID. Longer pages can be read in parts.

The content index and collection are also available as MCP resources. Results include source links.

This connection reads public content. It can’t edit the site, send messages, or install skills.

Prefer browsing? [Back to the website](<https://matthieu.pm/>).

# Project descriptions

Repository-based descriptions reviewed on 10 November 2026. These profiles cover the six projects listed on Matthieu's homepage. They explain the implementation and product choices visible in the project folders; they are not an assertion that every optional integration or feature is enabled on a public deployment. Product decisions below are supported by project documentation or by the implemented flow. No usage, revenue, learning-outcome, or research-result claims are implied.

## My collection

Website: https://matthieu.pm/inspirations

### Product and audience

My collection is a curated directory for designers, product builders, and design engineers. It brings together interface references, component libraries, development and AI tools, visual resources, utilities, and people worth following. The purpose is to help a visitor find something useful, understand its role, inspect a preview, and open the original resource. A separate My stack section shows tools Matthieu uses.

### Technology and architecture

The collection lives inside the matthieu.pm Bun and Turborepo monorepo. The web application uses Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, CSS Modules, shared UI components, and Geist typography, and is hosted on Vercel. Resource records are maintained in local JSON catalogues and assembled by a typed catalogue module. Each record carries a name, description, destination, and optional icon and preview. Navigation and counts derive from this data. A persistent client-side shell manages browsing controls and dialogs across category routes; local preferences keep view and sound choices consistent.

The same catalogue data feeds the public read-only MCP server. Its collection search supports keywords, categories, pagination, and original source links. Separate tools search and read published writing and skill guides. WebMCP exposes those read operations and bounded site navigation to compatible browsers. Markdown content negotiation and the LLM text exports provide additional text interfaces. These adapters reuse the site's data and published-content list rather than maintaining a separate catalogue. The collection does not need a user-account system or application database.

### Features

- Categories for inspiration, components, build tools, visuals, utilities, and designers.
- Global resource search, grouped sections, category navigation, and grid/list views.
- Resource artwork, expanded previews, external destinations, and useful fallbacks when media is missing.
- My stack previews, light/dark appearance, optional interaction sounds, and responsive navigation.
- Keyboard alternatives for previews and dialogs, Escape dismissal, focus restoration, and reduced-motion handling.
- A recognizable interactive glass-triangle identity and animated artwork, with source and licence notices retained.
- Read-only discovery through MCP, WebMCP, Markdown, and the full-text export.

### Product decisions

The content is curated rather than automatically scraped: short descriptions explain what each resource helps someone do. Categories follow function, and a resource can belong to more than one category; global search deduplicates destinations. Grid and list are two ways to browse the same records, so changing presentation does not change the resource set. Dense, restrained catalogue typography keeps scanning efficient, while expressive artwork gives the directory an identity. Preview and sound remain optional aids to exploration. Accounts, bookmarks, and submission workflows are outside the current browsing product. External sites remain references; the agent interfaces do not fetch them on the visitor's behalf.

## Atlas

Website: https://atlasapp.fr

### Product and audience

Atlas turns study materials into structured exam practice. It began around SKEMA Business School courses and lets learners upload their own documents, generate courses and lessons, practise questions at different difficulty levels, and see where they need more work. The core loop connects a learner's source material to repeated practice and visible progress.

### Technology and architecture

The application uses Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Bun, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui and Radix components, Framer Motion, and Recharts. Clerk supplies authentication. Convex is the current application backend and file-storage layer: its schema contains generated courses, lessons and questions, progress, files, token-usage logs, folders, tags, sharing, friendships, and study groups. Earlier PostgreSQL code and README references remain in the repository, but the current generation route and frontend provider use Convex.

Authenticated Next.js API routes coordinate document extraction and AI generation. PDF, DOCX, PPTX, and text inputs are converted to text; the generation pipeline analyzes the course structure, divides it into lessons, generates questions, validates the structured result, and persists the course in Convex. OpenAI's Responses API handles generation, with separate configurable defaults for course analysis and question generation. The default question strategy requests all difficulties together; incomplete or invalid results can fall back to per-difficulty generation. Usage checks and plan limits sit before generation, and the interface receives progress updates while work runs.

### Features

- Document uploads and AI-generated courses organized into lessons.
- Easy, medium, and hard practice, with explanations and structured single-choice, multiple-selection, and true/false question support in the generation model.
- Randomized quiz order, course progress, final tests, flashcard progress, XP, levels, and streaks.
- Analytics for accuracy, difficulty, course progress, weak areas, and recent activity.
- Folders, tags, file management, and account/usage settings.
- Course-sharing links, optional passwords and cloning permissions, friends, study groups, and leaderboards with privacy controls.
- English, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, and Chinese interface translations.

### Product decisions

The generation prompts explicitly constrain questions, answers, and explanations to the uploaded material. This keeps practice tied to the learner's course rather than a generic subject summary; it is a generation constraint, not a guarantee that model output is error-free. Difficulty levels and explanations support repeated practice, while analytics turn results into a next study action. Progress and social features give learners reasons to return without replacing the study task. Sharing and cloning make a generated course reusable, with controls over access and copying. Separating analysis from question generation and using a validated fallback balances generation cost, latency, and completeness. Storage and token allowances make expensive generation visible and bounded. No measured improvement in grades or learning outcomes is claimed.

## Atrium

Website: https://atriumcrm.com/

### Product and audience

Atrium is an AI-oriented CRM for revenue teams. It connects companies, contacts, deals, communication, enrichment, and follow-up work in one workspace. Its product direction is to make customer data actionable: users can structure the information their business needs, inspect the relevant context, and move from a record or segment to the next task without assembling that context across separate tools.

### Technology and architecture

The application uses Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, and Bun. Clerk manages identity and organizations; Convex stores workspace data and supplies reactive queries and mutations. An oRPC layer supports server operations. The interface uses Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui and Radix primitives, dnd-kit for reordering and drag/drop, React Flow for workflow surfaces, Recharts for reporting, and next-intl for localization.

The CRM model includes standard companies, contacts and deals, explicit relationships, custom attributes, custom objects, lists, and saved views. Attribute definitions and per-record values support business-specific schemas without turning every variation into a new hard-coded screen. Organization membership scopes workspace operations.

Pulse is the assistant entry point into that model. Its default execution path routes requests to specialists for CRM reads, CRM actions, research and enrichment, outreach, campaigns, lists/views, reporting, workflows, and record resolution. Specialists share grounded lookup helpers, scoped tools, handoffs, and persisted conversation state. The model layer supports configurable selection and routing; current Pulse model definitions use OpenAI routes, while Anthropic integration code also remains in the application. Provider, enrichment, communication, and billing integrations require their own configuration.

### Features

- Editable company and contact tables, custom fields, column ordering and visibility, filtering, saved views, and bulk operations.
- Deal pipelines with configurable stages and cards, inline editing, related-record lookups, and saved pipeline views.
- Custom objects with their own attributes and working views; lists for focused segments of a single object type.
- CSV import, duplicate-aware contact import, CSV/Excel export, archiving, and restore.
- AI attributes for classification, summarization, research, and custom prompts, including record-variable interpolation and bulk generation.
- Company/contact enrichment adapters, notes, activities, email/calendar context, campaigns, and email templates.
- Pulse-assisted record retrieval, proposed actions, outreach, reporting, workflow creation and execution, and duplicate-resolution workflows.
- Workspace membership, roles, account settings, and AI-usage tracking.

### Product decisions

Objects define record types; lists define working sets. Keeping those concepts separate lets teams adapt their workflow without fragmenting the underlying data. Related-record attributes put context in the table or pipeline where a decision is made. AI is connected to the CRM's records and actions rather than limited to free-form chat. Specialist routing gives distinct tasks explicit tool and context boundaries. Record resolution prepares and previews a merge; approved mutations are handed to the CRM-action specialist. Archiving provides a recoverable way to remove records from active work. Configurable views let different teams work over the same data in the form they need.

The code documents concrete limits: reporting changes require structured configuration; workflow edits need a grounded target and structured changes; some list/view actions depend on active UI context; direct deal enrichment is not supported by the enrichment specialist. Integration availability and enabled workflows depend on the workspace configuration.

## Carbon

Website: https://carbonhq.sh

### Product and audience

Carbon is a desktop home for coding agents. It puts multiple agent conversations beside their working directories, Git changes, pull requests, issues, and browser sessions. The intended user is a builder coordinating several coding tasks who needs to understand what each agent is doing and inspect its result. Carbon is based on Dray by yogesharc under Apache License 2.0; the repository records that upstream foundation and its third-party credits.

### Technology and architecture

The desktop application combines a React 19, TypeScript, and Vite renderer with a Tauri 2/Rust backend and Tokio-based asynchronous work. It wraps coding-agent CLIs, including Claude Code, Codex, fx, and pi, rather than implementing a model service in the portfolio website. Provider-specific harnesses adapt agent output and control flows to a shared conversation interface. The repository also contains a standalone Rust CLI, shared protocol types, a Next.js marketing site, and documentation.

The native backend owns processes, local files, Git operations, and services needed before the frontend exists. Sessions are persisted as JSONL event transcripts with a JSON session index; settings, drafts, attachments, and browser profiles have separate local stores. A local socket lets the Carbon CLI communicate with the running application. Remote-server support extends sessions to another machine, including Linux, and the embedded Chromium browser gives a session its own browsing context. Local transcription uses transcribe.cpp and downloaded speech models. GitHub and Linear integrations connect code and issue work to the conversation.

### Features

- Multiple sessions with agent/model selection, persistent conversation history, attachments, and saved task drafts.
- Per-session Git worktrees, branch selection, changes/diff inspection, pull-request context, and issue panels.
- Embedded browser tabs that can be prepared before a task and carried into the session.
- CLI operations for listing, creating, and messaging sessions and coordinating work between agents.
- Remote servers, browser automation commands, and development-server sharing.
- MCP server configuration, skill management, contextual mentions, and visible tool-permission prompts.
- Local dictation, interface/font preferences, subscription-usage indicators where providers expose them, and beta-update support.

### Product decisions

The session is the unit of work: conversation, branch, worktree, browser, and review context stay together. Separate worktrees make parallel tasks easier to inspect and reduce accidental interference between branches. Existing agent CLIs and their configurations remain the execution foundation, while Carbon supplies a consistent desktop workspace around them. Local transcript storage keeps work resumable and inspectable without requiring Carbon to host conversations; agent providers and explicitly used integrations still receive the requests needed for their services. The CLI makes coordination available to agents as well as people. Local speech processing keeps dictation audio on the machine.

Release status and boundaries matter: the repository records a macOS beta release. Pages/Spaces code is feature-gated and disabled by default, so it should not be presented as a generally available feature. Provider capabilities and edit/replay behavior vary; for example, latest-prompt replay is restricted to eligible text-only Codex turns.

## Forge

Website: https://app.forgenow.tech/

### Product and audience

Forge is an issue-tracking and agent workspace for software teams. It connects incoming work, personal execution, team planning, documents, and agent-assisted actions in a shared product available through the web and a macOS host. The central idea is that an agent should work with the same issues and workspace context as the team, while people retain a clear view of proposed changes and their results.

### Technology and architecture

The current application uses TanStack Start and Router, React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui/Base UI components, and Tiptap editing. A Bun/Turborepo workspace separates the application, shared packages, and services. Better Auth manages authentication and organizations. Neon Postgres and Drizzle hold canonical product data; a contract-first oRPC layer and OpenAPI 3.1 describe the public API. The Electron Forge macOS shell hosts the same renderer and brokers the official local Codex app-server.

Authenticated server commands own issue creation and editing, membership checks, relations, revisions, and retry receipts. Bounded authorized queries supply team and personal issue views; client caches are projections of server state rather than a second authoritative database. Legacy browser data has a resumable import path. Revision checks support visible conflict resolution. Durable PostgreSQL jobs provide identity, leases, checkpoints, retry budgets, and recovery, while the Workflow SDK handles application-owned durable business workflows.

Agent execution runs through a separate EVE service. Product capabilities remain behind the application authorization boundary, and material writes require approval and idempotency. Generated code runs in isolation without application or model-provider credentials. Provider eligibility, usage accounting, and spending controls are explicit policies rather than assumptions made by the renderer.

### Features

- Inbox triage, My Issues tabs, team issue views, filters, ordering, and paginated queries.
- Issue detail editing, statuses, priorities, assignees, labels, sub-issues, relationships, comments, activity, reactions, subscriptions, and attachments.
- Workspace/team planning surfaces for projects, cycles, initiatives, saved views, documents, and templates, subject to their owning rollout gates.
- A full Forge conversation workspace and a compact Ask Forge panel over the current page, with thread history and approval cards.
- Meeting transcript, recap, note, and follow-up surfaces, with native import dependent on provider OAuth and scheduled synchronization.
- Scoped API credentials, documented API contracts, and idempotent resource creation.
- Shared-renderer macOS integration and a local Codex broker; configured cloud execution uses the separate runtime.

### Product decisions

Human edits and agent actions use the same canonical product services so permissions, validation, history, and retries have one source of truth. My Issues is derived from the authenticated actor's assignments, authorship, and subscriptions, rather than a separate personal task database. Approval is attached to the action and its authority; a chat response alone is not evidence that a mutation happened. Durable receipts and transactional commands make retries safer, while explicit conflicts protect concurrent editing. Sharing the renderer keeps the desktop and web product aligned instead of maintaining two independent interfaces. Server feature gates keep unfinished or unqualified integrations from looking available.

The repository labels the current build unreleased. Some modules have implemented server-backed paths but require rollout and deployment qualification. Signals and Reviews are restricted to explicitly granted, fictional read-only previews. Inbound external MCP is documented as gated work. Resources, Loops, and other optional modules should not be described as universally enabled merely because their code exists. Provider qualification and hosted acceptance are separate from local or fixture tests.

## Researchie

Website: https://survey.matthieu-pm.chatgpt.site

### Product and audience

Researchie presents a research questionnaire as a conversation. It supports exploratory work on how people use AI assistants, judge outcomes, check and repair results, and set boundaries for delegation. Participants move through one question at a time using inline choices or written replies; researchers receive structured, versioned responses for needs discovery and scenario design.

### Technology and architecture

The implementation uses React, TypeScript, shadcn/ui and Radix-based components, Tailwind CSS, Next-compatible App Router source, and a Vinext/Vite execution setup. Cloudflare D1 stores data through Drizzle's SQLite schema. The hosted Sites environment supplies researcher authentication; participant response links can be used without an account.

A versioned questionnaire in `lib/survey.ts` defines question wording, answer types, and deterministic branching. The conversational component renders the current eligible question, while the survey API validates and persists responses. The schema separates studies, survey responses, sessions, and optional publication-update contacts. Participant mutations use a random response token whose hash is stored on the server. A browser-tab session retains the token for resume and withdrawal. Researcher access controls listing and export. The protocol and complete instrument document what each question is intended to establish.

### Features

- Consent, recent-task recall, intended success, checking, correction and recovery, effort, consequences, control, delegation, and priorities in one linked questionnaire.
- Different paths for participants with a recalled task, those who cannot recall one, and those who have not used AI.
- Conditional follow-ups, optional skips, inline choices, written answers, and answer review before submission.
- Autosave and same-tab resume; reopening an earlier answer resets later answers so branch conditions remain consistent.
- Participant answer downloads and withdrawal, researcher participant links, and CSV/JSON export.
- Separate preview responses excluded from normal exports, versioned records, and event history for interpretation.
- Optional, separately consented publication-update email signup, stored apart from survey exports and deleted with a withdrawn response.

### Product decisions

The chat presentation makes a structured form approachable, while fixed wording and deterministic branches keep the research instrument reviewable and comparable. Follow-ups stay anchored to one recalled task before asking broader preferences, which helps preserve the participant's own account. Earlier-answer edits invalidate later answers rather than silently retaining responses to an inapplicable branch. Account-free participation reduces entry friction; authenticated researcher access keeps management and export separate from participation. Notification consent is separate from research participation and does not change the survey answers.

This is a conversational survey, not a live generative interviewer. The protocol identifies it as an owner-private pilot: recruitment information and retention arrangements require finalization before broader recruitment. Recalled behavior and self-reported effort do not establish observed performance, causal effects, predictive validity, or validated trust scores. Event timing includes interruptions. The tab-scoped resume token can be lost when the tab closes. Publication-update email delivery is not automated. These boundaries are part of the product and research design, not measured study findings.
